"caption": "《The 6:55 Express》，1990年，铝上焊接钢和青铜，14 x 21 x 5英寸 图片由詹姆斯·吉布森提供", "credit": "ARTnews", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "同年，即1968年初，吉布森遇到了当地商人威廉·恩德雷斯（William Endres），后者曾报名参加他的艺术课，后来向吉布森提供了他在卡诺瓦市（Kanawha City）的金属车间设施的钥匙，以便将他的雕塑材料从木材扩展到更多金属作品中。在那里，吉布森还在使用各种不同金属的过程中精进他的焊接技能。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "尽管吉布森早期的创作题材通常以鸟类为中心，但他后几年的作品将焦点转移到了神话上，这在随后的十年中变得更为突出。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "1970年，吉布森前往中田纳西州立大学（MTSU）为艺术系开发雕塑项目。在那里，学院完善的雕塑设施让吉布森能够相当专注地推进他的雕塑实践。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/G1996HA1-image.jpg?w=400", "alt": "", "caption": "《Hell on Wheels I》，1996年，黄铜和铝上焊接钢，10 x 21 x 7英寸 图片由詹姆斯·吉布森提供", "credit": "ARTnews", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在最初的几年里，即1970–74年间，这位艺术家创作了惊人的70件新雕塑，并在纽约和纳什维尔举办了5场大型个展，确立了吉布森作为艺术家的声誉。此外，他在1974年赢得了竞争激烈的“第一美国银行”（First American Bank）雕塑委任项目，为纳什维尔市中心的新广场制作一座喷泉。", "links": [{"text": "fountain", "url": "https://website-jamesgibson.artlogic.net/content/feature/30/artworks-2736-fountain-1974/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这种丰硕的创作势头得以延续，在1975–79年间创作了70多件作品，并举办了2场个展、完成了2项重大委任项目，其中包括1975年为纳什维尔奇克伍德植物园（Cheekwood Botanical Gardens）制作的焊接黄铜喷泉，以及为西弗吉尼亚州亨廷顿美术馆（Huntington Galleries）“鸟类步道”（Bird Walk）自然步道入口创作的户外“门户”雕塑。后者或许最清晰地反映了吉布森中期创作中诸如女性人形、鸟类以及形而上反射器等核心母题。", "links": [{"text": "fountain", "url": "https://website-jamesgibson.artlogic.net/content/feature/30/artworks-2746-fountain-1975/"}, {"text": "portal", "url": "https://website-jamesgibson.artlogic.net/content/feature/30/artworks-2758-nature-walk-portal-1976/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/G1982RR-image.jpg?w=400", "alt": "", "caption": "《Rites of Passage》，1982年，焊接钢，15 x 12 x 9英寸 图片由詹姆斯·吉布森提供", "credit": "ARTnews", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "吉布森艺术生涯的崛起与他在课堂上的成功直接挂钩。“如果我的教学进展顺利，我的雕塑就会进展顺利，”吉布森经常这样评价。他对工艺的这种执着并没有被忽视，他在1980年晋升为全职教授，以表彰他作为艺术家和教师十年来所展现出的卓越水平。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《田纳西人报》（The Tennessean）的艺术与戏剧评论家克拉拉·海罗尼穆斯（Clara Hieronymus）当时将吉布森描述为“理想教师艺术家的原型。也就是说，他自己的创作才华说明了他正在向学生传授的内容；他既是老师又是受人尊敬的艺术家。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "随后的十年（1980–89年）延续了这一精神，吉布森为23场展览和5项委任项目创作了120多件雕塑。其中两场展览——一场在奇克伍德的纳什维尔植物园与美术中心（Nashville Botanical Gardens and Fine Arts Center of Cheekwood），另一场在查尔斯顿的国会大厦文化中心综合体（Cultural Center capitol complex）——展出了形而上反射器、写作机器以及门户等作品。", "links": [{"text": "one", "url": "https://website-jamesgibson.artlogic.net/exhibitions/58-cheekwood-fine-arts-center-solo-exhibition/"}, {"text": "another", "url": "https://website-jamesgibson.artlogic.net/exhibitions/59-the-cultural-center-solo-exhibition/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/G2001VG-image.jpg?w=400", "alt": "", "caption": "《Virginia Gianino》，2001年，雕刻彩绘木雕，17 x 7 x 4英寸 图片由詹姆斯·吉布森提供", "credit": "ARTnews", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“‘形而上学’这个词简单来说就是‘超越化学’。当古希腊人进入超越物理现实的事物——那些无法被触摸、品尝、看见、闻到或听到的事物时，他们称之为形而上学，”吉布森在解释这个概念时说道。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在80年代初期，他的作品变得更具实验性，例如创作出兼具桌子功能的雕塑。吉布森开始质疑艺术可以是什么，并在物体的功能性中发现了一种不同种类的意义：“桌子可能是在考虑到与雕塑相同的个人、主观理念的情况下制作的，但它的观看方式会有所不同。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "延续这一势头，吉布森的一些大型雕塑在1982年世界博览会（1982 World's Fair）上的一场大型户外国外展览中找到了舞台。随后，沃尔特斯州立社区学院（Walters State Community College）、田纳西大学（University of Tennessee）和克利夫兰州立社区学院（Cleveland State Community College）也迅速举办了其他户外雕塑展。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/G2009BD-image.jpg?w=400", "alt": "", "caption": "《Burden Carrier》，2009年，雕刻彩绘木雕，59 x 24 x 10英寸 图片由詹姆斯·吉布森提供", "credit": "ARTnews", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "所有这些机遇最终汇聚成了吉布森该时期最重要的委任项目——为中田纳西州立大学（MTSU）1986年75周年校庆创作的雕塑《Rites of Passage》。“融入我最新作品《Rites of Passage》中的理念，一直是我近期创作的主要催化剂。关于周期的理念——出生、生活、死亡。人类这种动物总是在寻找重复，寻找某种可以信仰的事物，”吉布森在谈到这件作品时说道。", "links": [{"text": "Rites of Passage", "url": "https://website-jamesgibson.artlogic.net/content/feature/30/artworks-2949-rites-of-passage-1986/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "他在中田纳西州立大学（MTSU）的最后十年里，创作了90多件雕塑、举办了20场展览、完成了5项委任项目，这些作品通常由焊接钢、黄铜、青铜或铝以及多种金属混合制成。1991年和1996年，他的作品在坎伯兰画廊（The Cumberland Gallery）的两场展览中亮相，并继续在各大户外面展中展出。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/G1990MA-image.jpg?w=400", "alt": "", "caption": "《Mayday Trapping》，1990年，焊接钢、青铜与铝，4 x 11 x 4英寸，图片由詹姆斯·吉布森提供", "credit": "ARTnews", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "吉布森的大型作品《Big Table》在查塔努加州立技术社区学院（Chattanooga State Technical Community College）举办的1995–96年第三届雕塑公园双年展（Sculpture Garden III Biennial Exhibit）上斩获采购奖，而他的《WV Buffet》雕塑则入选了1995年第五届国际鞋盒雕塑大赛（International Shoebox Sculpture Competition），现被查尔斯顿大学永久收藏。1997年，他受托创作的不锈钢雕塑《Reflection of Memories》完工并安装在查尔斯顿大学的克莱大厦（Clay Tower Building）。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "吉布森这样描述他那时的创作：“深受我对雕塑形式、神话以及作为显眼路标以指引旅行者的隐喻的兴趣所影响。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "不久之后的1999年，吉布森在中田纳西州立大学（MTSU）任教29年后退休。2000年，该校授予吉布森荣誉退休教授称号。他还入选了查尔斯顿大学的校友成就画廊（Alumni Gallery of Achievement），其作品被美国各地的私人及公共收藏机构，以及土耳其、德国和奥地利的收藏机构所收藏。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/G1992A1-image.jpg?w=400", "alt": "", "caption": "图片由詹姆斯·吉布森提供", "credit": "ARTnews", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "退休后，吉布森的作品主题再次转变，从精神通道和渡船转向了墓碑和石标的形态。2003年，纳什维尔的弗里斯特视觉艺术中心（Frist Center for the Visual Arts）在一场以田纳西州艺术家为核心的展览结束后，将《Mardis Marker》购入其永久收藏。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "吉布森生前创作的最后一件作品取名自圣经经文《4:14 St. James Place》，预示了他自己在2017年以81岁高龄走向死亡的旅程。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "吉布森为他的社区留下了不可磨灭的印记，拥有丰富的文化遗产和包含600多件雕塑的宏大作品集。如今，他遗产中的240件作品正面向收藏家和画廊进行出售。", "translated": true}]
article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "With a career spanning 60 years, James Gibson was a revered Tennessee teacher and sculptor. Today, over 240 sculptures from his estate are available to collectors for purchase.", "links": [{"text": "James Gibson", "url": "https://www.jamesgibsonsculptor.com/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "It’s hard to miss a sculpture by James Gibson , whose numerous and often massive works can be characterized by blocky abstracted, yet continuous forms, constructed in either wood or metal, sometimes both. Though Gibson is known for his extensive oeuvre of more than 600 sculptures, he also had a rich 60-year career as a college art professor in the American South.", "links": [{"text": "James Gibson", "url": "https://www.jamesgibsonsculptor.com/"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/G1986RG-image.jpg?w=400", "alt": "", "caption": "Photo Courtesy of MTSU", "credit": "ARTnews"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Born in Charleston, West Virginia, in 1937, Gibson earned a Master of Fine Art degree in sculpture from Ohio University in 1961 and, that same year, he began his teaching career at Furman University in Greenville, South Carolina. In 1963, he returned to West Virginia to join the Salem College faculty as head of the art department. Morris Harvey College then offered Gibson an opportunity to return to Charleston as a member of the art department faculty in the fall 1965. Gibson taught there for the next five years, while he worked on wood carvings, and welded sculpture."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "During this time in West Virginia, Gibson’s work caught the attention of the Charleston Art Gallery at Sunrise, the first major art gallery to exhibit his work. Gibson also completed three notable commissions : a brass sculpture-fountain for the FMC Inorganic Chemical Company’s newly constructed open-air atrium garden in South Charleston in 1966, two large brass sculptures for permanent installation at the Morris Harvey College campus in 1967, and a brass sculpture for the entrance of the remodeled Lewis Chevrolet dealership in 1968.", "links": [{"text": "commissions", "url": "https://website-jamesgibson.artlogic.net/commissions/all"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/G1990EX-image.jpg?w=400", "alt": "", "caption": "The 6:55 Express , 1990, Welded Steel and Bronze on Aluminum, 14 x 21 x 5” Photo Courtesy of James Gibson", "credit": "ARTnews"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "That same year, in early 1968, Gibson met local businessman William Endres, who had enrolled in one of his art classes and later offered Gibson the key to his own metal shop facilities in Kanawha City to expand his sculptural materials from wood to include more work in metal. There, Gibson also refined his welding skills while working with many different metals."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Though Gibson’s early subject matter often centered around birds, his work in later years shifted focus to mythology, which became more prominent in the following decade."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In 1970, Gibson moved to develop a sculpture program for the art department at Middle Tennessee State University (MTSU). There, the extensive sculpture facilities at the college allowed Gibson to focus quite intensely on furthering his sculpture practice."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/G1996HA1-image.jpg?w=400", "alt": "", "caption": "Hell on Wheels I , 1996, Welded Steel on Brass and Aluminum, 10 x 21 x 7” Photo Courtesy of James Gibson", "credit": "ARTnews"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In his first few years, between 1970–74, the artist produced a whopping 70 new sculptures, with five major solo exhibitions in New York and Nashville that established Gibson’s reputation as an artist. Additionally, he won the competitive First American Bank sculpture commission in 1974 for a fountain at the new plaza in downtown Nashville.", "links": [{"text": "fountain", "url": "https://website-jamesgibson.artlogic.net/content/feature/30/artworks-2736-fountain-1974/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "This fruitfulness continued, with more than 70 works produced between 1975–79 for two solo exhibitions and two major commissions, including a welded brass fountain for Nashville’s Cheekwood Botanical Gardens in 1975 and an outdoor “ portal ” sculpture for the entrance of to the Huntington Galleries Bird Walk nature trail in West Virginia. The latter perhaps most acutely reflected such dominant motifs in Gibson’s midcareer work as female figures, birds, and metaphysical reflectors.", "links": [{"text": "fountain", "url": "https://website-jamesgibson.artlogic.net/content/feature/30/artworks-2746-fountain-1975/"}, {"text": "portal", "url": "https://website-jamesgibson.artlogic.net/content/feature/30/artworks-2758-nature-walk-portal-1976/"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/G1982RR-image.jpg?w=400", "alt": "", "caption": "Rites of Passage , 1982, Welded Steel, 15 x 12 x 9” Photo Courtesy of James Gibson", "credit": "ARTnews"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The rise in Gibson’s art career was directly tied to his success in the classroom. “If my teaching goes well, my sculpture goes well,” Gibson often remarked. This commitment to his craft did not go unnoticed, with a promotion by 1980 to a full-time professorship that recognized his ten years of excellence as an artist and a teacher."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Clara Hieronymus, the Art and Drama Critic for the Tennessean , characterized Gibson at the time as “the prototype of the ideal teacher artist. Which is to say that his own creative talents speak for what he is teaching his students; that he is both teacher and respected artist.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "That sentiment was captured in the subsequent decade from 1980­–89 in the more than 120 sculptures Gibson made for 23 exhibitions and five commissions. Two exhibitions, one at the Nashville Botanical Gardens and Fine Arts Center of Cheekwood and another at the Cultural Center capitol complex in Charleston included metaphysical reflectors, writing machines, and portals.", "links": [{"text": "one", "url": "https://website-jamesgibson.artlogic.net/exhibitions/58-cheekwood-fine-arts-center-solo-exhibition/"}, {"text": "another", "url": "https://website-jamesgibson.artlogic.net/exhibitions/59-the-cultural-center-solo-exhibition/"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/G2001VG-image.jpg?w=400", "alt": "", "caption": "Virginia Gianino , 2001, Carved and Painted Wood, 17 x 7 x 4” Photo Courtesy of James Gibson", "credit": "ARTnews"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“The word metaphysics simply means ‘beyond the chemical.’ When the Greeks got into things that were beyond the physical reality – things that could not be touched, tasted, seen, smelled, or heard – they called it metaphysical,” Gibson explained of the concept."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "During the early ‘80s his work became more experimental, with sculptures that could also function as a table, for example. Gibson began questioning what art could be , finding a different kind of meaning in an object’s functionality: “a table may be made with the same kind of personal, subjective idea in mind that a piece of sculpture is, but it’s not going to be looked at in the same way.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Continuing this momentum, some of Gibson’s larger sculptures found a stage at the 1982 World’s Fair in an expansive outdoor exhibition. Other outdoor sculpture exhibitions quickly followed at Walters State Community College, the University of Tennessee, and Cleveland State Community College."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/G2009BD-image.jpg?w=400", "alt": "", "caption": "Burden Carrier , 2009, Carved and Painted Wood, 59 x 24 x 10” Photo Courtesy of James Gibson", "credit": "ARTnews"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "All of these opportunities culminated into Gibson’s most significant commission of the period, Rites of Passage , the sculpture for MTSU’s 75th anniversary celebration in 1986. “The idea that went into my latest work Rites of Passage has been the major catalyst in my work lately. article_text:
With a career spanning 60 years, James Gibson was a revered Tennessee teacher and sculptor. Today, over 240 sculptures from his estate are available to collectors for purchase.

It’s hard to miss a sculpture by James Gibson , whose numerous and often massive works can be characterized by blocky abstracted, yet continuous forms, constructed in either wood or metal, sometimes both. Though Gibson is known for his extensive oeuvre of more than 600 sculptures, he also had a rich 60-year career as a college art professor in the American South.

Born in Charleston, West Virginia, in 1937, Gibson earned a Master of Fine Art degree in sculpture from Ohio University in 1961 and, that same year, he began his teaching career at Furman University in Greenville, South Carolina. In 1963, he returned to West Virginia to join the Salem College faculty as head of the art department. Morris Harvey College then offered Gibson an opportunity to return to Charleston as a member of the art department faculty in the fall 1965. Gibson taught there for the next five years, while he worked on wood carvings, and welded sculpture.

During this time in West Virginia, Gibson’s work caught the attention of the Charleston Art Gallery at Sunrise, the first major art gallery to exhibit his work. Gibson also completed three notable commissions : a brass sculpture-fountain for the FMC Inorganic Chemical Company’s newly constructed open-air atrium garden in South Charleston in 1966, two large brass sculptures for permanent installation at the Morris Harvey College campus in 1967, and a brass sculpture for the entrance of the remodeled Lewis Chevrolet dealership in 1968.

That same year, in early 1968, Gibson met local businessman William Endres, who had enrolled in one of his art classes and later offered Gibson the key to his own metal shop facilities in Kanawha City to expand his sculptural materials from wood to include more work in metal. There, Gibson also refined his welding skills while working with many different metals.

Though Gibson’s early subject matter often centered around birds, his work in later years shifted focus to mythology, which became more prominent in the following decade.

In 1970, Gibson moved to develop a sculpture program for the art department at Middle Tennessee State University (MTSU). There, the extensive sculpture facilities at the college allowed Gibson to focus quite intensely on furthering his sculpture practice.

In his first few years, between 1970–74, the artist produced a whopping 70 new sculptures, with five major solo exhibitions in New York and Nashville that established Gibson’s reputation as an artist. Additionally, he won the competitive First American Bank sculpture commission in 1974 for a fountain at the new plaza in downtown Nashville.

This fruitfulness continued, with more than 70 works produced between 1975–79 for two solo exhibitions and two major commissions, including a welded brass fountain for Nashville’s Cheekwood Botanical Gardens in 1975 and an outdoor “ portal ” sculpture for the entrance of to the Huntington Galleries Bird Walk nature trail in West Virginia. The latter perhaps most acutely reflected such dominant motifs in Gibson’s midcareer work as female figures, birds, and metaphysical reflectors.

The rise in Gibson’s art career was directly tied to his success in the classroom. “If my teaching goes well, my sculpture goes well,” Gibson often remarked. This commitment to his craft did not go unnoticed, with a promotion by 1980 to a full-time professorship that recognized his ten years of excellence as an artist and a teacher.

Clara Hieronymus, the Art and Drama Critic for the Tennessean , characterized Gibson at the time as “the prototype of the ideal teacher artist. Which is to say that his own creative talents speak for what he is teaching his students; that he is both teacher and respected artist.”

That sentiment was captured in the subsequent decade from 1980­–89 in the more than 120 sculptures Gibson made for 23 exhibitions and five commissions. Two exhibitions, one at the Nashville Botanical Gardens and Fine Arts Center of Cheekwood and another at the Cultural Center capitol complex in Charleston included metaphysical reflectors, writing machines, and portals.

“The word metaphysics simply means ‘beyond the chemical.’ When the Greeks got into things that were beyond the physical reality – things that could not be touched, tasted, seen, smelled, or heard – they called it metaphysical,” Gibson explained of the concept.

During the early ‘80s his work became more experimental, with sculptures that could also function as a table, for example. Gibson began questioning what art could be , finding a different kind of meaning in an object’s functionality: “a table may be made with the same kind of personal, subjective idea in mind that a piece of sculpture is, but it’s not going to be looked at in the same way.”

Continuing this momentum, some of Gibson’s larger sculptures found a stage at the 1982 World’s Fair in an expansive outdoor exhibition. Other outdoor sculpture exhibitions quickly followed at Walters State Community College, the University of Tennessee, and Cleveland State Community College.

All of these opportunities culminated into Gibson’s most significant commission of the period, Rites of Passage , the sculpture for MTSU’s 75th anniversary celebration in 1986. “The idea that went into my latest work Rites of Passage has been the major catalyst in my work lately. The idea of a cycle – birth, life, death. The human animal always looks for repetition, something to have faith in,” Gibson said of the work.

His final decade at MTSU included the creation of more than 90 sculptures, 20 exhibits, and five commissions, typically made from welded steel, brass, bronze, or aluminum, and a mixture of metals. In 1991 and 1996, his work was presented in two exhibitions at The Cumberland Gallery and continued to be featured in outdoor shows.

Gibson’s massive Big Table received the purchase award at the 1995–96 Sculpture Garden III Biennial Exhibit at Chattanooga State Technical Community College, while his WV Buffet sculpture was accepted in the 1995 fifth International Shoebox Sculpture Competition, where it is currently housed in the permanent collection at the University of Charleston. In 1997, his commissioned stainless-steel sculpture Reflection of Memories was realized and installed at the University of Charleston’s Clay Tower Building.

Gibson characterized his work at this time as “strongly influenced by my interest in sculptural form, mythology, and marker as a metaphor for a conspicuous object serving as a guide for travelers.”

Shortly thereafter, in 1999, Gibson retired after 29 years of teaching at MTSU. In 2000, the same school named Gibson professor emeritus. He was also inducted into the Alumni Gallery of Achievement by the University of Charleston and his work can be found in both private and public collections throughout the United States, as well as Turkey, Germany, and Austria.

In retirement, Gibson’s work shifted again from themes of spiritual passage and ferries, giving way to forms of grave markers and cairns. In 2003, the Frist Center for the Visual Arts in Nashville purchased Mardis Marker for its permanent collection following an exhibition centered on Tennessee artists.

The last work Gibson made, titled 4:14 St. James Place , taken from a Bible verse, anticipated his own passage to death in 2017 at 81 years old.

Gibson left behind an indelible mark on his community, with a rich cultural legacy and a robust portfolio of more than 600 sculptures. Today, 240 of those works in his estate are available for purchase to collectors and gallerists.

article_text:
Tony award winner Lois Smith has joined the cast of Colin West ’s upcoming feature “ Outside of Cleveland .”

Smith’s first on-screen role was in 1955 opposite James Dean in “East of Eden.” She has appeared in such films as “Five Easy Pieces,” “Twister,” “Minority Report,” “Dead Man Walking,” “Ladybird” and “The French Dispatch.”

In 2017, Smith starred as the title character in Michael Almereyda’s “Marjorie Prime,” receiving Gotham and Independent Spirit nominations for best supporting actress among other accolades.

Related Stories

Netflix Grapples With Digital-Ad Squeeze Amid Widening Glut of Streaming Commercials

‘Gordon,’ a Big Netflix Series From Argentina, Unpacked by Pablo Trapero and Star Rodrigo de la Serna

On stage, Smith was nominated for Tonys for her performances in “The Grapes of Wrath” and “Buried Child,” and she won the Tony Award for “The Inheritance.”

She also has numerous TV credits ranging from “Law & Order: Organized Crime” to “Ray Donovan,” “The Americans” and “True Blood.”

“Outside of Cleveland” follows Max, a jingle writer in Chicago who wonders where his life went. When his parents sell his childhood home outside of Cleveland, he drives back to help them pack. He then wakes up in the winter of 2009, aged 18.

Back in his senior year, he reconnects with his neighbor Ellie, who encourages him to write his own songs. Max begins to wonder whether he has been sent back to change his past or to say goodbye to it.

Smith will play Max’s grandmother Marjorie.

“Lois’s character is named after my own grandmother who passed away in 2012. She was someone who always told me the truth, even when I didn’t always want to hear it. This is the same role that Marjorie fills in our film,” said West.

“She isn’t there to comfort Max or make things easier; she’s there to tell him the truth. The character needed to be tough yet warm, and Lois embodies that. She had such a wonderful attitude throughout, and she brought tears to my eyes on more than one occasion. Having a legend like her bring my grandmother’s spirit to the screen means more to me than I can say.”

“Colin wrote such a beautiful character in Marjorie. There’s an immediate familiarity to her: that combination of a grandmother’s warmth and wisdom. It’s a pivotal moment in the film, and we needed someone who could convey its emotional weight with real authenticity,” said producers Dan Erdman, Chad Simpson, Heather Francis and Drew Johnson in a joint statement.

“Lois was a dream choice, and we couldn’t be more thrilled to have her.”

Casting director Findley Davidson added: “The word is overused, but it’s apt here: Lois Smith is an icon. At 95, she continues to work non-stop across theater, TV and film, and her dedication to the craft is remarkable.”

“Outside of Cleveland” also stars Alex Wolff , Brooklynn Prince, Jim Gaffigan, Sarah Wayne Callies and Michael Ian Black.

As pointed out by West, at the 2017 Gotham Awards, Prince and Smith were among the youngest and oldest nominees ever for “The Florida Project” and “Marjorie Prime” respectively.

“Years later, they end up in the same movie,” he enthused.

West’s film, selected for the U.S. in Progress co-production forum at Poland’s Tauron American Film Festival , is produced by Brain Scratch Productions, 1515 Films and Sub_Sequential Pictures. His previous, “Linoleum,” premiered at SXSW.

“The cast always hinged on Max’s character, so that’s where we started. Alex Wolff was an immediate choice as not only is he an incredible musician, he can also convey both the world-worn weariness of adulthood and the spark of adolescence, often within the same scene,” he said.

“From there, since the story moves fluidly between two timelines without relying on gimmicks, I needed actors who could make the family feel lived-in from the first frame. Jim, with whom I’d worked before, and Sarah possess that warmth and humor, and Brooklynn brings an honesty and maturity that’s rare at any age. Lois ended up being the final key to that family dynamic and I was thrilled to see it all come together seamlessly.”

West isn’t hiding that the story he’s telling is very personal.

“It’s always hard to put that much of yourself on screen, and there were days on set in Ohio that almost felt a little too close to home. When I entered Max’s room after our production design team had finished with it, I saw actual items from my own childhood. My art team had asked my parents for items, and it freaked me out, but also brought a smile to my face.”

He added: “Making any form of art should always be part exploration and part excavation, and this was the perfect combination of the two. Once I stopped trying to hide from the personal, the film became more relatable and honest. When I watch it, I see the Ohio that I know and love. I see home. And I am deeply indebted to my team for making that happen.”

退屈することを何よりも嫌うガキ大将の少年・石田将也。ある時、彼の学校に聴覚障害を持つ少女・西宮硝子が転校してくる。硝子の存在に好奇心を抱き、そのおかげで退屈な日々から解放された将也だったが、硝子との間に起こったある出来事をきっかけに、将也は周囲から孤立してしまう。それから5年。心を閉ざして生き、高校生になった将也は、いまは別の学校へ通う硝子のもとを訪れる。 脚本は「たまこラブストーリー」や「ガールズ＆パンツァー」を手がけた吉田玲子が担当。声の出演は、将也役に「言の葉の庭」の入野自由、硝子役に「あの日見た花の名前を僕達はまだ知らない。」の早見沙織。そのほか悠木碧、小野賢章、金子有希、石川由依、潘めぐみ、豊永利行らが共演し、小学生時代の将也役を俳優の松岡茉優が務めている。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": 映画 聲の形

劇場公開日： 2026年10月30日

映画館を探す

予告編を見る

U-NEXTで 本編を見る PR

解説・あらすじ

「週刊少年マガジン」に連載され、「このマンガがすごい！」や「マンガ大賞」などで高い評価を受けた大今良時の漫画「聲の形」を、「けいおん！」「たまこラブストーリー」などで知られる京都アニメーションと山田尚子監督がアニメーション映画化。 退屈することを何よりも嫌うガキ大将の少年・石田将也。ある時、彼の学校に聴覚障害を持つ少女・西宮硝子が転校してくる。硝子の存在に好奇心を抱き、そのおかげで退屈な日々から解放された将也だったが、硝子との間に起こったある出来事をきっかけに、将也は周囲から孤立してしまう。それから5年。心を閉ざして生き、高校生になった将也は、いまは別の学校へ通う硝子のもとを訪れる。 脚本は「たまこラブストーリー」や「ガールズ＆パンツァー」を手がけた吉田玲子が担当。声の出演は、将也役に「言の葉の庭」の入野自由、硝子役に「あの日見た花の名前を僕達はまだ知らない。」の早見沙織。そのほか悠木碧、小野賢章、金子有希、石川由依、潘めぐみ、豊永利行らが共演し、小学生時代の将也役を俳優の松岡茉優が務めている。

2016年製作／129分／G／日本 配給：松竹 劇場公開日：2026年10月30日

その他の公開日：2016年9月17日（日本初公開）

原則として東京で一週間以上の上映が行われた場合に掲載しています。 ※映画祭での上映や一部の特集、上映・特別上映、配給会社が主体ではない上映企画等で公開されたものなど掲載されない場合もあります。

article_text:
EXCLUSIVE: Bella Glanville has signed with Established Artists .

The British model and Geek Girl actress joins the roster of international talents on the books at Established, and will be represented by Tonja René.

Glanville, who is based in L.A., was most recently in Chad Ferrin’s Sunset Strip Killers , playing one of the victims of real-life serial killers Doug Clark and Carol Bundy. She was also shortlisted at the BAFTA Film Awards for Best Short Film for her short Imperfect Cadence and had a recurring role in Seasons 1 and 2 of Netflix’s Geek Girl .

Away from the screen, she is an international model and has fronted campaigns for the likes of Coca-Cola, Stella Mccartney, Valentino and Adidas and appeared on the covers of magazines such as Vogue.

Watch on Deadline

For Established Artists, the signing is a third this month. It added actress, writer, director and producer Natasha Ofili, who acted in Creed III and The Politician , to its ranks for representation soon after it signed Anne-Marie MacKay, veteran writer-producer and co-founder of Propaganda Films, for management.

Patrick Havern launched Established Artists in 2021 as a full service talent management company.

editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "皮埃尔-伊夫·德拉努瓦（Pierre-Yves Delannoy）致力于羊毛与拼贴、毛毡与刺绣的创作，并在毁灭中探寻乌托邦。如今，他入围了“年轻一代艺术奖”（Young Generation Art Award）短名单。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "阳光透过慕尼黑英国花园北缘不远处的多马格园区（Domagk-Areal）工作室的落地窗洒进来。在阳光下的一个小型支架上，放着一块羊毛白的绒头小片，桌上则放着另一块浓郁浆果色的绒头小片。皮埃尔-伊夫·德拉努瓦于1995年出生于法国香槟沙隆，长期以来一直在进行羊毛与毛毡实验。就在最近，他首次使用了自己晒干的胭脂虫来进行染色。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "刺绣、羊毛创作以及拼贴技法在他的作品中扮演着重要角色。他的图像世界具象化，且常常带有自传性质。在慕尼黑美术学院他的导师、电影艺术家朱利安·罗斯费尔德（Julian Rosefeldt）门下，他因此占据了某种特殊地位。这也给他留出了很大空间，因为其他学生主要都在电脑前创作。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "然而，人们在他的母题中也能清晰地识别出电影元素。例如，当他从一辆私家车的内部展现法国乡村无尽的田野和筒仓时，正如他在毛毡壁挂作品《骄傲的寄生虫》（Fières pouilleux）中所做的那样。随后，他将目光引向那片兼作秘密露宿约会地点的电影感荒凉之地。在《当田野燃烧》（Pendant que les champs brûlent）中，他悼念着一片早已被毁坏的前工业化自然。这种失落被他当作个人伤痛来对待。但这种痛苦的惋惜，与德拉努瓦作品中显现的一种乌托邦紧密相连——“怀揣着这样一种希望：如果我用泪水浇灌这片土地，未来或许就能在那里生根发芽”。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "表演性纺织品", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在小巧却充满氛围的工作室里喝着咖啡时，他讲述道，自己目前正专注于羊毛与绵羊的来源。在欧洲，羊毛几乎已经不划算，羊毛脂宁可被烧掉，这比清洗和梳理它们以便进一步加工还要便宜。只有极少数极具排他性的羊毛供应商才会重新麻烦起来，像传统那样定期将绵羊从西班牙南部的冬牧场转移到北方。但正是这种对地形的依恋，吸引着德拉努瓦。", article_text:
Pierre-Yves Delannoy arbeitet mit Wolle und Collagen, mit Filz und Stickerei und sucht die Utopie in der Zerstörung. Nun steht er auf der Shortlist für den Young Generation Art Award

Die Sonne scheint durch die Fensterfront des Ateliers auf dem Domagk-Areal, nicht weit entfernt vom nördlichen Rand des Englischen Gartens in München. Auf einem kleinen Ständer liegt im Sonnenlicht ein flauschiges Läppchen in Wollweiß, auf einem Tisch ein anderes in einem satten Beerenton. Pierre-Yves Delannoy, geboren 1995 im französischen Châlons-sur-Marne, experimentiert schon lange mit Wolle und Filzen. Gerade hat er erstmals selbst getrocknete Kaktusläuse zum Färben verwendet.

In seinen Werken spielen Stickerei, das Arbeiten mit Wolle und Collagetechniken eine Rolle. Seine Bildwelten sind figurativ und haben oft einen autobiografischen Hintergrund. Bei seinem Professor, dem Filmkünstler Julian Rosefeldt, an der Akademie der Bildenden Künste München hatte er damit eine gewisse Sonderstellung. Und viel Platz, denn die anderen Studierenden arbeiteten hauptsächlich am Computer.

Doch kann man auch bei seinen Motiven durchaus filmische Elemente erkennen. Zum Beispiel, wenn er die endlosen Felder und Silos des ländlichen Frankreichs aus dem Innenraum eines Pkw zeigt, wie in der gefilzten Wandarbeit "Fières pouilleux" (Stolze Verlauste). Dann lenkt er den Blick auf die kinematografische Einöde, die zugleich als geheimer Cruising-Treffpunkt dient. In "Pendant que les champs brûlent" (Während die Felder brennen) trauert er um eine längst zerstörte vorindustrielle Natur. Dieser Verlust wird von ihm wie eine persönliche Wunde behandelt. Doch das schmerzliche Bedauern ist geknüpft an eine in Delannoys Werk spürbare Utopie, "an die Hoffnung, dass, wenn ich dieses Land mit meinen Tränen tränke, dort eine Zukunft keimen könnte".

Performative Textilien

Gerade sei er mit der Herkunft der Wolle und der Schafe beschäftigt, erzählt er bei einem Kaffee in seinem kleinen, aber atmosphärischen Arbeitsraum. In Europa lohne sich Wolle kaum noch, da werden die Vliese lieber verbrannt, das sei billiger, als sie für die Weiterverarbeitung zu waschen und zu kämmen. Nur sehr exklusive Wolllieferanten machen sich wieder die Mühe, die Schafe regelmäßig von der Winterweide im Süden Spaniens bis in den Norden zu bringen, wie es Tradition ist. Aber genau diese Verbundenheit mit der Topografie ist es, die Delannoy interessiert.

In seinem Atelier hat er gerade ungewaschene Wolle, in der noch jede Menge Strohreste stecken, gewaschen und gekämmt. "Ich habe gemerkt, wie viel Arbeit das ist, aber es war auch ein bisschen magisch – wie kochen oder backen oder einen Teig machen." Seit Generationen sind seine Familienmitglieder Bäcker in der Champagne. In seinen Performances filzt er live, die Decken hängt er über Gestänge und kreiert so temporäre Architekturen. Neulich, sagt er, sei ihm eingefallen, dass er bereits als Kind Höhlen aus Filzdecken gebaut habe. Die Arbeit mit Wolle und Textil sei traditionell eher weiblich und vergleichsweise wertlos konnotiert. Delannoy widersetzt sich dem Klischee. "Wenn die Stücke größer sind, dann wird es auch körperlich richtig anstrengend. Aber die Technik gefällt mir sehr, sie hat etwas Performatives."

Pierre-Yves Delannoy hat in seiner Arbeitsweise einen ganz eigenen künstlerischen Ausdruck gefunden, doch thematisch ist seine Bandbreite groß. Auf normale Kassenzettel aus der Drogerie oder dem Biomarkt stickt er Dickpics, die ihm unaufgefordert gezeigt werden. Als wolle er dieser digitalen Übergriffigkeit etwas Langsames, Aufmerksames entgegensetzen, das bleibt.

Was ist der Young Generation Art Award?

Eine Karriere starten? Nachhaltig von der Kunst leben können? Für viele junge Künstlerinnen und Künstler, die den Abschluss der Kunsthochschule in der Tasche haben, ist das ein Traum. Der Young Generation Art Award zielt auf diese Phase, in der sich oft die Weichen stellen. Für den Preis, den das Unternehmen Degussa Goldhandel gemeinsam mit dem Monopol-Magazin vergibt, können sich internationale Künstlerinnen und Künstler bis zum Alter von 35 Jahren bewerben.

Aus über 600 Einsendungen wurden fünf Künstlerinnen und Künstler für die aktuelle Shortlist ausgewählt . Hope Bartley, Joanna Chia-yu Lin, Pierre-Yves Delannoy, Joana Loewis und Louisa Pieper werden ab dem 27. November ihre Werke in der Degussa Niederlassung am Berliner Gendarmenmarkt zeigen. Die Jury aus Yilmaz Dziewior, Direktor des Museums Ludwig in Köln, der Kuratorin Maya Heckelmann sowie Elke Buhr, Chefredakteurin von Monopol, wählt die Gewinnerin oder den Gewinner aus. Die Preisverleihung erfolgt im Februar 2027. Der Young Generation Art Award ist mit 10.000 Euro dotiert. Doch auch schon die Shortlist ist mit einem Preis verbunden: Jede Nominierung wird mit 3000 Euro ausgezeichnet. Wir stellen die Künstlerinnen und Künstler der Shortlist nacheinander bei Monopol vor .

Dieser Artikel erschien zuerst in Monopol 11/2026.

editorial_excerpt_zh: 恶作剧的时代：这位巴西作者导演做客节目，讨论他的最新力作——一部对过去与地方细节进行无尽创新挖掘的作品
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "本周播客带来对巴西电影人克莱伯·门多萨·菲略的深度访谈，他的最新剧情片《秘密特工》目前正在部分影院上映。该片是今年戛纳电影节（门多萨在此斩获最佳导演奖）以及今年秋季纽约电影节的亮点。与该导演的许多电影一样，《秘密特工》的故事背景设定在他在巴西东北部的家乡累西腓，时间是1977年——正如开场不久的一块字幕所告诉我们的那样，“这是一个恶作剧的时代”。瓦格纳·马拉（戛纳最佳男演员得主）饰演马塞洛，他是一个正在逃避与统治军事独裁政权相关的强大势力追捕的男人，正试图与一群乌合之众般的异见人士和政治流亡者一起寻找避难所以及离开该国的可能安全通道。《秘密特工》是一部对过去与地方的特定细节进行无尽创新、生动且令人惊悚的挖掘之作。正如这位电影人近期的作品，包括尖锐的类型混合片《巴克劳》（2019年，与儒利亚诺·多尔内莱斯联合导演）以及自传性质的纪录片《幽灵图片》（2023年）一样，它深深迷恋于电影的历史与无限可能。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《电影评论》编辑德维卡·吉里什和克林顿·克鲁特就这部电影、他将故事设定在熟悉地点的倾向、他对录音技术以及来自过去的声音的迷恋，以及他是如何在这部令人不寒而栗的政治惊悚片中巧妙融合奇幻与幽默等话题，采访了门多萨。", "translated": true}]

article_text:
This week’s Podcast features an in-depth interview with Brazilian filmmaker Kleber Mendonça Filho, whose latest feature, The Secret Agent , is in select theaters now. The film was a highlight of both this year’s Cannes, where Mendonça won the Best Director prize, and this fall’s New York Film Festival. The Secret Agent is set, like many of the director’s films, in his Northeastern Brazilian hometown of Recife, in 1977—“a time of mischief,” as a title card tells us early on. Wagner Moura (Cannes Best Actor winner) plays Marcelo, a man on the run from powerful forces connected to the ruling military dictatorship, seeking refuge and possible safe passage out of the country with a ragtag group of dissidents and political exiles. The Secret Agent is an endlessly inventive, lively, and frightening excavation of the specifics of past and place. And like the filmmaker’s recent work, including the scathing genre hybrid Bacurau (2019, co-directed by Juliano Dornelles) and the autobiographical documentary Pictures of Ghosts (2023), it’s in thrall to the history and possibilities of cinema.

Film Comment Editors Devika Girish and Clinton Krute spoke to Mendonça about the film, his tendencies to set his stories in familiar locales, his fascination with recording technology and voices out of the past, and how he managed to blend fantasy and humor into this chilling political thriller.
excerpt_original: Times of mischief: the Brazilian auteur joins to discuss his latest, an endlessly inventive excavation of the specifics of past and place

"放置在冷藏间的陈设增强了这种矛盾感。这艘船暗示了一个方向、一个彼岸，却又被禁锢在一个用于保存和静止的封闭空间中。其形态预示着一种本应由环境所暂停的运动。作品标题《A-Riva》同样处于这一门槛之上，既让人联想到靠岸，又同时保留了一种未竟航程的可能。因此，这座雕塑在两种状态之间摇摆不定：一种是延续官方记忆的纪念碑，另一种是能够驶向不同目的地的船只。大海虽缺席，却在船体中、在殖民航线的记忆中、以及在想象中的旅程与尚未完成的旅程之间的距离中重现。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": article_text:
Il blu si distende sulle mappe, attenua le coste, lascia affiorare minuti punti sulla carta. Avvicinandosi, la superficie rivela piccole depressioni, segni impressi dal peso del piombo: tracce di naufragi nel Mediterraneo, coordinate di viaggi interrotti. Nella Ghost Trip Series di Austin Camilleri (Malta, 1972), lo sguardo oscilla tra la visione d’insieme e il dettaglio, tra la geografia riconoscibile e la singolarità di un’impronta. La carta si fa fondale, il disegno sprofonda mentre i punti resistono all’evanescenza. È da questa materia che germoglia CHap(ə)l , una mostra in cui la storia affiora attraverso le superfici, le loro alterazioni, ciò che rimane visibile e ciò che continua a premere sotto la soglia della visione.

Nella sala principale della galleria 10 & zero uno , i ganci dell’ex macelleria, ancora utilizzati per appendere le opere, mantengono visibile la funzione precedente dello spazio. La loro presenza introduce una seconda trama di segni, inscritta nell’architettura e riattivata dall’allestimento. Come le impronte sulla carta, anche questi elementi appartengono a una storia d’uso che sopravvive al mutamento. Il passato rimane incorporato nelle cose, mentre a cambiare è il modo in cui vengono guardate.

Nella Passport Series , Camilleri interviene sulle pagine del proprio passaporto coprendo con inchiostro rosso le informazioni personali e i timbri. Sotto la campiture le scritture continuano a trasparire e, sul retro, la carta conserva le impronte lasciate al torchio dalle piccole cartucce di piombo utilizzate anche nelle mappe. Il documento resta riconoscibile ma la sua funzione si incrina: ciò che certifica un’identità e regola l’attraversamento dei confini diventa una superficie in cui le informazioni vengono oscurate e il segno si deposita altrove. L’identità si sottrae così alla leggibilità amministrativa, mentre la materia conserva le tracce di ciò che la cancellazione non riesce a eclissare del tutto.

Nella Ghost Trip Series , quelle stesse impronte passano dal documento individuale alle mappe dei naufragi di imbarcazioni migranti nel Mediterraneo. Disegni e collage vengono sommersi dall’inchiostro blu, che ne attenua i contorni fino a sospenderli tra veduta marina e fondale. I punti impressi interrompono la dissolvenza, non potendo ricostruire le rotte né restituire i corpi scomparsi, localizzando però il luogo della perdita e sottraendolo almeno in parte all’indistinzione del mare. Tradizionalmente strumento di orientamento e controllo, la cartografia si misura così con ciò che non riesce a ricomporre.

Nel testo che accompagna la mostra, Lucia Longhi richiama le Songlines delle culture aborigene australiane, percorsi attraverso cui il territorio si lega alla trasmissione di conoscenze e memorie. Il riferimento alimenta l’idea di mappa come racconto, in cui i punti custodiscono relazioni, passaggi e forme di sapere. Nelle opere di Camilleri, tuttavia, il punto assume anche una valenza più perturbante, segnando la frattura di un percorso, la distanza tra una rotta tracciata e un approdo mancato. Mentre il blu sommerge il paesaggio, il piombo trattiene sulla carta la precisione di una perdita, lasciando emergere la tensione tra la capacità di localizzare un evento e l’impossibilità di restituirne interamente la storia.

È nella distribuzione della visibilità che passaporto e mappe rivelano la propria complementarità. Il primo regola chi può muoversi e sotto quale identità; le seconde registrano gli esiti di attraversamenti che non hanno raggiunto la destinazione. Il piombo collega le due serie attraverso una medesima pressione, mentre il rosso copre e il blu sommerge, modificando ciò che può essere letto. A emergere è allora una contraddizione: gli strumenti che organizzano il movimento e rendono il mondo intelligibile possono anche delimitare ciò che merita riconoscimento, lasciando altre esistenze ai margini o consegnandole alle sole coordinate di una tragedia.

Questa tensione assume una forma tridimensionale in A-Riva , opera inedita collocata nella vecchia cella frigorifera della galleria. L’effigie della regina Vittoria, ispirata alla statua di Republic Square, già Piazza Regina, a La Valletta, si prolunga nella carena di un’imbarcazione. Il volto della sovrana e lo scafo formano un unico corpo scolpito in legno di tulipier. La figura, tipicamente consegnata alla fissità del monumento, entra così nella struttura stessa della navigazione saldando il potere coloniale al mezzo attraverso cui ha esteso le proprie rotte e consolidato il dominio sui territori.

La nave, ciò nonostante, custodisce una storia ambivalente. Strumento di conquista ed espansione, è stata anche luogo di lavoro, conflitto, fuga e resistenza. Il riferimento all’ Hydrarchy , concetto elaborato dagli storici Peter Linebaugh e Marcus Rediker, permette di leggere il confronto tra il potere marittimo organizzato dall’alto e le forme di autorganizzazione dei marinai. In A-Riva le due forze convivono nella stessa figura: da un lato il volto della sovrana rimane saldato alla carena, dall’altro la trasformazione del monumento in imbarcazione ne sovverte la fissità simbolica. L’autorità non viene semplicemente rovesciata, trovandosi costretta a condividere la propria forma con un mezzo che porta con sé anche la possibilità di sottrarsi al controllo.

La collocazione nella cella frigorifera accentua questa ambivalenza. La nave suggerisce una direzione, un altrove, eppure resta trattenuta in uno spazio chiuso destinato alla conservazione e all’immobilità. La sua forma promette un movimento che l’ambiente sospende. Anche il titolo A-Riva si colloca su questa soglia, evocando l’approdo e lasciando aperta al contempo la possibilità di una traversata incompiuta. La scultura rimane così in bilico tra due condizioni, quella del monumento che perpetua una memoria ufficiale e quella dell’imbarcazione che può orientarsi verso una destinazione diversa. Il mare è assente ma ritorna nella carena, nella memoria delle rotte coloniali e nella distanza tra il viaggio immaginato e quello ancora da compiere.

In CHap(ə)l , il potere si manifesta negli oggetti attraverso cui organizza la vita, il movimento e la memoria. Camilleri interviene su dispositivi già carichi di storia, alterandone la funzione e rendendone visibili le contraddizioni. Dal passaporto alle mappe, fino alla figura ibrida di A-Riva , le opere interrogano le condizioni che rendono possibile un attraversamento e i sistemi che ne stabiliscono il valore. Anche lo spazio espositivo partecipa a questa lettura: i ganci rimasti alle pareti e la cella frigorifera riconvertita conservano le tracce di funzioni precedenti, così come la carta trattiene le pressioni del piombo. La materia non restituisce il passato intatto ma ne custodisce le impronte, rendendole disponibili a nuove interpretazioni. È in questo scarto tra ciò che permane e ciò che può ancora cambiare che si apre lo spazio della contestazione.

article_text:
Scarier than reality, the widely circulated Mitch McConnell silicone mask whispers into Mia Stern ’s ear about the turning political tides seen in both the US midterm elections and online life

‘They’re shooting Mitch McConnell out of a cannon tomorrow.’ Or at least, so claimed a viral tweet on the evening of 3 November as the results of the American midterm elections rolled in. A ‘blue tsunami’ was coming into view. And the eighty-four-year-old Republican senator from Kentucky, not even up for reelection, was now its unlikely mascot.

The signs were there. Last month, images of a silicone mask of McConnell started making the rounds online. An Instagram carousel published by Howard Senft Studios , whose account is otherwise filled with silicone masks and CGI renders of horror movie characters, showed the senator’s face propped up on a stick and seen from the front and in three-quarter profile with Oingo Boingo’s Dead Man’s Party (1985) playing in the background. Among the hundreds of comments were many iterations of the same idea: that the mask ‘looks too alive’ compared to the real thing. Glassy-eyed, mouth ajar, skin pale and mottled, and overall looking like a limp slice of ham with some glasses and a combover, the copy does have more meat to it than the original.

Listen, this guy is very old and, by my standards, very evil. First elected to the US Senate in 1984, McConnell is the second longest-serving senator currently in office (behind Chuck Grassley, the Republican from Iowa, who is also the oldest serving senator at the age of ninety-three) and was the longest-ever serving Senate party leader. The ‘World Wide Web’ was only invented five years into his first term. So McConnell is no stranger to online mockery, having been frequently compared to SpongeBob’s Baby Prunes for his signature tight-lipped smile and empty gaze, or to a turtle. Throughout his Senate career, spanning Reagan to Trump, McConnell became known as a sly tactician and a thorn in the side of Democrats. Nicknamed ‘Dr No’, he repeatedly opposed reforms for affordable healthcare, gun regulation and campaign-funding regulation, and he blocked the vote on Obama’s Supreme Court nominee. His easy yeses: a federal abortion ban and acquitting Trump in his two impeachment trials. What McConnell voted for, administration after administration, was instrumental in affirming hardline Republican policies and shaping the current conservative-majority Supreme Court that has, among others, overturned Roe v. Wade, expanded rights to carry firearms and clamped down on affirmative action.

Posting the McConnell mask a couple of weeks before Halloween and the midterms on a horror-filled Instagram account is a pretty unsubtle way to call the Senator a monster. Where a political caricature might emphasise and deform traits to arrive to the same conclusion, the mask here relies on hyperrealism, the punchline being that reality is about as scary as it can get. Dressing up as a famous politician or character type for the sake of parody is nothing new – and belongs to a broader tradition of using costume to subvert ‘normality’ and social order. Historically, there’s a double nature to wearing a mask that both allows wearers to embody a new identity and to protect their own, making it an effective tool of critique. Hyperrealism, too, has its place in social critique. During the French Revolution, wax heads of Jacques Necker and the Duc d’Orléans were commissioned from Philippe Curtius and his pupil Marie Grosholtz (later and better known as Madame Tussaud) to parade around on spikes in protests years before they started decapitating politicians for real.

Lift the monster’s mask and what’s underneath is the lingering presence of white American conservative power. Following his hospitalisation for a fall earlier this year, McConnell was wheeled back to Congress, where he has been mostly nonverbal, as if, in a Weekend at Bernie’s- type stunt, the Senator’s dead body was being used as a dummy to enact Republican policies. That’s not too far from the truth: The New York Times counts 47 times in the leadup to the midterm elections that Trump asked voters to pretend he himself was on the ballot, as if each individual Republican candidate were mere meat puppets for the MAGA host.

A week before the elections, a mask of another Trump-adjacent figure, Susan Dell, cofounder and chair of the Michael & Susan Dell Foundation, appeared on Senft’s page. Dell had become an internet sensation after appearing at the White House for an event promoting the ‘Trump Accounts’ (‘tax-advantaged investment accounts for US citizens under 18’) towards which her foundation committed $6.25 billion. The reason for her sudden fame was her serious case of Mar-a-Lago face (similar to a mask except the silicone goes straight into the face), which drew comparisons to that of two Trump-nominated government officials, Barbera Thornhill and Kelly Loeffler. Pictures of the trio, their skin stretched impossibly thin across their skull, caught on. Was the current administration hiding aliens in plain sight?! Such cod-conspiratorial overtones speak to a broader irreverence. As trust in the truth of internet media collapses under the weight of ever-proliferating generative AI, good-old fake news and popular discrediting of traditional sources of information, the only way to react might be to lean so far into it as to turn it into a tragicomic joke. In the face of it all, Senft’s silicone masks are a refreshingly tactile nod to old school conspiracy: like a behind-the-scenes look at the skinsuit factory.

The dark humour that underpins the whole understanding of the McConnell mask is a strand of what is now called ‘dark woke’, a hardening up of the left’s style of communication that also coincides with, in the US, Democratic campaigns that have shifted their focus more clearly towards citizens’ material conditions. Democrats have a history of suffering from an off-putting condescending attitude. What works with the mask – this quasi- grotesque body , where the Rabelaisian ‘guiltless flesh’, as Julia Kristeva describes it , is instead fake and inscribed with moral guilt – is that everybody’s in on the joke. Tens of thousands of people coalesced around it in a carnivalesque act of derision of power. And the midterm results have spoken: the absurdity of the current administration can only be met with a programme that puts people first, sure – but also with brash and collective mockery. Pantagruelism is back ; the kids will be alright.
